text: A language model API does one thing: it takes text and returns text. Everything else in a real product, which text goes in, what is done with the reply, and what happens when something fails, belongs to the harness. The model is the engine and the harness is the rest of the car, and two teams using exactly the same model can ship products of very different quality because their harnesses differ.

The harness first assembles the context from parts: the system instructions, descriptions of the tools, retrieved passages, the conversation so far, and the new message. The context window is a fixed budget measured in tokens, so packing it is like packing a suitcase with a weight limit. Essentials go in first, and when space runs out the harness drops the least valuable items, such as the oldest turns or the lowest ranked passages, but never the instructions themselves.

The order of the parts matters as well. Models tend to use information at the start and end of a long context more reliably than material buried in the middle, so the strongest passages belong near the edges. And because providers can cache the work done on a prefix that repeats exactly, the parts that never change, such as instructions and tool descriptions, should come first, with the parts that change on every request placed after them.

When the reply will be read by code rather than a person, the harness asks for structured output, usually JSON that must match a schema, a precise description of the fields and their types. It then validates what comes back. If validation fails, the harness sends the error message back to the model and asks again, a small number of times at most. Some providers can also constrain decoding directly, masking any token that would break the required format.

Failures also come from the outside world: requests time out and providers apply rate limits. The standard response is to retry with exponential backoff, waiting one second, then two, then four, with a little randomness added, called jitter, so that thousands of clients do not all retry at the same instant, rather like a crowd leaving a stadium through staggered exits. Retrying is only safe for requests that do no harm if they run twice.

Finally, a good harness records everything. Every call is logged as a trace that holds the assembled input, the raw output, the token counts, the latency and the cost. Traces make failures debuggable after the fact, and they become the raw material for evaluation, because the questions real users actually asked are the best test cases you will ever get.

Seen this way, the harness turns a probabilistic text generator into a dependable software component. Once the harness lets the model choose which tool to call next, runs it, and feeds the result back in a loop, the system has become an agent. Building that loop properly, with its tools, errors and stopping rules, is the next lesson.
